# Research Design

## Research Topic and Motivation

\small

**Research question**

- Do more negative 10-K disclosures lead to a different stock market reaction around the filing date?
- We use filing-window **cumulative abnormal returns**, $\mathrm{CAR}[-1,+1]$, as the market reaction measure.

\vspace{0.15cm}

**Why 10-K tone matters**

- 10-K filings contain both accounting numbers and qualitative disclosures.
- Part I and Part II discuss business conditions, risks, legal exposure, MD&A, and financial performance.
- More negative language may indicate adverse information or higher perceived risk.
- Investors may respond to this information around the filing date.

\vspace{0.15cm}

**Main variables**

- **y variable:** filing-window CAR
- **X variable:** negative tone in 10-K Part I and Part II


# Construction of Variable X

## Definition and Measurement of Variable X

\small

**Definition**

- Negative tone is measured at the firm-year level from each 10-K filing.

\vspace{0.15cm}

$$
\mathrm{NegTone}_{i,t}
=
\frac{\mathrm{Negative\ words}_{i,t}}{\mathrm{Total\ words}_{i,t}}
$$

\vspace{0.15cm}

**Measurement choice**

- Negative words are identified using the Loughran-McDonald financial sentiment dictionary.
- The dictionary is designed for financial and accounting texts.
- This is more suitable than a general sentiment dictionary for 10-K filings.

\vspace{0.15cm}

**Text scope**

- We focus on Part I and Part II of the 10-K filing.
- These sections contain business description, risk factors, MD&A, and financial discussion.
- They are directly relevant to investor interpretation of firm risk and performance.


## Construction Process of Variable X

\small

**Starting point**

- Begin with the firm-year 10-K sample.
- Key identifiers include CIK, report year, filing date, filing URL, and accession information.

\vspace{0.2cm}

**Text preparation**

- Download 10-K filing texts from SEC EDGAR.
- Cache filing texts locally to avoid repeated downloads.
- Extract Part I and Part II where possible.
- Use a documented full-text fallback if section extraction fails.

\vspace{0.2cm}

**Tone calculation**

- Tokenize the extracted text.
- Count total words and Loughran-McDonald negative words.
- Calculate $\mathrm{NegTone}_{i,t}$ for each firm-year filing.
- Export the tone measure for merging with CAR and firm-level controls.


## Full-Sample Text Processing and Sampling

\small

- De-duplicated input: 160,816 firm-year filing rows from 2002 to 2024.
- Cleaning is applied before tone calculation to avoid repeated filings and non-10-K placeholders.

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Main cleaning rules**

\vspace{-0.08cm}

\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.12}
\begin{tabularx}{0.94\textwidth}{p{0.27\textwidth} p{0.16\textwidth} X}
\hline
\textbf{Case} & \textbf{Handling} & \textbf{Rationale} \\
\hline
Different filing date 
& Keep 
& Likely valid 10-K or transition filing. \\

Multiple series / asset pools / trusts 
& Drop 
& Often not ordinary listed operating firms. \\

Same filing date and same text count 
& De-duplicate 
& Likely repeated collection or repeated submission. \\

Non-10-K placeholder 
& Drop 
& Not formal 10-K text; would contaminate tone. \\

Same filing date but different text 
& Drop from main regression 
& May include amendments, exhibits, or extraction variants. \\
\hline
\end{tabularx}

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Sampling design**

- Stratified yearly sampling: 1,500 observations per report year.
- Final sampled input: 34,500 firm-year rows across 23 report years.
- Filing date is preserved as the event date for the CAR merge.


## Sampling Summary

\small


- Processing all 160,816 filings is time-consuming.
- Stratified yearly sampling keeps coverage across the full 2002--2024 period.
- The design avoids over-representing years with more filings.

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Sampling metrics**

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.15}
\begin{tabular}{lr}
\hline
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{Value} \\
\hline
Report-year range & 2002--2024 \\
Rows before sampling & 160,816 \\
Sampled rows & 34,500 \\
Sampling rule & 1,500 per report year \\
Average sampling rate & 21.51\% \\
Sampling-rate range & 19.52\% in 2009 to 23.81\% in 2002 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Date distinction**

- **Report year:** used for sampling and firm-year grouping.
- **Filing date:** used as the event date for CAR construction and merge.

\small

**Purpose**

- Summarizes the dictionary-based tone output before the regression merge.
- Core variables: negative tone, total words, and negative words.
- Describes both tone intensity and text extraction coverage.

\vspace{0.15cm}

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.15}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrr}

\textbf{Variable} & \textbf{Mean} & \textbf{Median} & \textbf{Std. dev.} & \textbf{Min} & \textbf{Max} \\
\hline
NegativeTone & 0.017981 & 0.017592 & 0.007988 & 0 & 0.118142 \\
Total words & 28,596.633 & 23,983 & 23,318.390 & 6 & 235,876 \\
Negative words & 552.889 & 430 & 500.646 & 0 & 5,302 \\
\hline

\vspace{0.15cm}

**Interpretation**

- A higher $\mathrm{NegTone}$ means a larger share of negative financial words in the relevant 10-K sections.
- The wide range of total words reflects variation in filing length and text extraction coverage.


# Construction of Variable y

## Definition of Variable y

\small

**Dependent variable**

::: columns
::: {.column width="65%"}

\vspace{0.2cm}

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{CAR}_{i}[-1,+1] &= AR_{i,-1} + AR_{i,0} + AR_{i,+1} \\
AR_{i,t} &= R_{i,t} - R_{m,t}
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
::: {.column width="35%"}

\footnotesize
\textbf{where:}

\vspace{0.05cm}

\begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
$R_{i,t}$: & firm daily return \\[0.25em]
$R_{m,t}$: & market daily return \\[0.25em]
$t=0$: & 10-K filing date
\end{tabular}

:::
:::

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Interpretation**

- $\mathrm{CAR}[-1,+1]$ measures the cumulative abnormal return around the 10-K filing date.
- It captures the short-term stock market reaction to the filing.
- A lower CAR indicates a more negative market reaction around the filing date.

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Why CAR?**

- The research question studies market response to negative 10-K tone, and stock returns directly reflect investor reaction.
- Abnormal returns remove general market-wide movements, making the measure more firm-specific.
- The short $[-1,+1]$ window captures possible anticipation and delayed reaction while reducing noise from unrelated events.


## Data Source for CAR Construction

\small

**Main platform: WRDS**

\vspace{0.3cm}

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}

**CRSP daily stock file**

- Provides firm-level daily stock returns
- Used to obtain $R_{i,t}$
- Return data are retrieved around each 10-K filing date

\vspace{0.3cm}

**CRSP value-weighted market return**

- Used as the market benchmark return
- Used to obtain $R_{m,t}$
- Allows market-adjusted abnormal return calculation

:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

**SEC / 10-K filing data**

- Provides filing date and CIK
- Filing date defines the event date:
  
  $$
  t=0
  $$

\vspace{0.3cm}

**Why CIK-to-PERMNO linking is needed**

- 10-K filings are identified by CIK
- CRSP stock returns are identified by PERMNO
- CIK must be linked to PERMNO before stock returns can be retrieved

:::
:::


## Matching CAR with Negative Tone

\small

**Input from text-based tone construction**

- Sampled 10-K observations
- Calculated LM negative tone
- CIK and filing date

\vspace{0.08cm}

**y-variable construction**

- Link CIK to PERMNO
- Retrieve CRSP daily returns around the filing date
- Calculate daily abnormal returns
- Sum abnormal returns into $\mathrm{CAR}[-1,+1]$

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Final merge**

- Merge CAR back to the negative-tone dataset
- Keep observations with both tone data and valid return data
- The final regression sample is based on filings with matched X and y


## Sample Construction Limitation

\small

**Main issue**

- The text sample was drawn before CRSP coverage was checked.
- A CIK-PERMNO availability table was not used before sampling.
- As a result, the text sample included firms without usable stock return data.

\vspace{0.08cm}

**During the X-y matching process**

- Some firms had no valid PERMNO.
- Some firms were not covered by CRSP.
- Some filing dates had no usable return data.
- Only around 40\% of text observations could be matched to return data.

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Interpretation and future improvement**

- This is a sample-construction limitation, not a CAR calculation error.
- A better workflow would first restrict the universe to firms with CRSP coverage, and then draw the 10-K text sample.


# Empirical Method and Results

## Empirical Method

\small

**Main regression**

$$
\mathrm{CAR}_i[-1,+1]
=
\alpha
+
\beta \cdot \texttt{LM\_NegTone}_i
+
\gamma \cdot \mathrm{Controls}_i
+
\mathrm{YearFE}
+
\mathrm{IndustryFE}
+
\varepsilon_i
$$

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Main hypothesis**

- $\beta < 0$: a negative $\beta$ would suggest that more negative 10-K tone is associated with lower filing-window CAR.

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Datasets merged**

- **X variable:** LM negative tone from 10-K filings
- **y variable:** $\mathrm{CAR}[-1,+1]$, renamed from `car_vw_m1_p1`
- **Controls:** Compustat firm-level variables

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Final regression sample**

- 13,243 observations
- 5,841 firms
- Sample period: 2002--2024


## Regression Specification

\small

**Control variables**

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Firm-level controls**

- Firm size
- Book-to-market
- Leverage
- ROA
- Loss dummy
- Text length

:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Fixed effects**

- Year fixed effects
- Two-digit SIC industry fixed effects

\vspace{0.08cm}

**Purpose**

- Controls account for firm characteristics that may affect stock returns.
- Fixed effects absorb common year-level and industry-level variation.

:::
:::

\vspace{0.2cm}

**Interpretation of** $\beta$

- $\beta$ captures the association between 10-K negative tone and filing-window CAR.
- If $\beta$ is significantly negative, the result supports the hypothesis that negative tone is related to lower market reaction.


## Main Regression Results

\small

**Coefficient on** \textbf{\texttt{LM\_NegTone}}

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}
\begin{tabular}{lr}
\hline
\textbf{Specification} & \textbf{Coefficient} \\
\hline
Tone only & -0.112 \\
With controls & 0.069 \\
Controls + FE & 0.156 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.2cm}

**Main finding**

- The coefficient on negative tone is not statistically significant.
- After adding firm-level controls, the result remains insignificant.
- We do not find strong evidence that negative tone predicts filing-window CAR.
- The result suggests limited immediate market reaction to negative 10-K tone in our sample.


## Interpretation and Limitations

\small

**Interpretation**

- Insignificant results do not necessarily mean that the hypothesis is wrong.
- Instead, the evidence does not show a statistically reliable relationship in this sample.
- The market reaction to 10-K tone may be weaker or more difficult to detect than expected.

\vspace{0.2cm}

**Possible explanations**

- The matched regression sample is relatively small, which may reduce statistical power.
- 10-K information may already be anticipated by investors before the filing date.
- Market reaction may occur outside the $[-1,+1]$ event window.
- Negative tone may reflect routine risk disclosure rather than new bad news.
- Firm-level controls may absorb part of the information contained in tone.
- Tone levels may be less informative than changes in tone over time.


# Robustness Tests and Conclusion

## Purpose of Robustness Tests

\small

**Why robustness tests are needed**

- The baseline result shows no significant relation between $\texttt{LM\_NegTone}$ and $\mathrm{CAR}[-1,+1]$.
- Robustness tests check whether this result depends on specific sample or measurement choices.

\vspace{0.2cm}

**Main robustness concerns**

- **Event-window choice:** Is the result driven by the specific $[-1,+1]$ window?
- **Text-scope choice:** Does the result change when tone is measured from different 10-K sections?
- **Sample composition:** Is the result driven by specific types of firms or by outliers?

\vspace{0.2cm}

**Robustness checks**

- Use alternative event windows: $\mathrm{CAR}[0,+1]$ and $\mathrm{CAR}[-2,+2]$.
- Test alternative text sections such as Part I, Part II, and Item 1A Risk Factors.
- Exclude financial firms and utilities.
- Winsorize extreme values.


## Robustness Test 1: Alternative Event Windows

\small

**Purpose**

- The baseline model uses $\mathrm{CAR}[-1,+1]$.
- We test whether the conclusion changes under alternative filing-window definitions.

\vspace{0.2cm}

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\hline
 & $\mathbf{CAR[-1,+1]}$ & $\mathbf{CAR[0,+1]}$ & $\mathbf{CAR[-2,+2]}$ \\
\hline
$\texttt{LM\_NegTone}$ & 0.157 & 0.098 & -0.045 \\
Standard error & (0.172) & (0.162) & (0.198) \\
Significant at 5\% & No & No & No \\
Observations & 13,279 & 13,279 & 13,279 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.15cm}

**Interpretation**

- $\texttt{LM\_NegTone}$ is not statistically significant across event windows.
- The baseline conclusion is therefore not driven by the specific $[-1,+1]$ window.


## Robustness Test 2: Sample Restrictions and Winsorization

\small

**Purpose**

- Financial firms and utilities may differ from ordinary operating firms.
- Extreme values may mechanically affect regression estimates.
- We therefore restrict the sample and winsorize extreme values.

\vspace{0.2cm}

\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.15}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\hline
 & $\textbf{Baseline}$ & $\textbf{Excl. Fin. \& Util.}$ & $\textbf{+ Winsorize}$ \\
\hline
$\texttt{LM\_NegTone}$ & 0.157 & 0.292 & 0.290 \\
Standard error & (0.172) & (0.211) & (0.182) \\
Significant at 5\% & No & No & No \\
Observations & 13,279 & 9,761 & 9,761 \\
$R^2$ & 0.012 & 0.015 & 0.020 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.15cm}

**Interpretation**

- Excluding financial firms and utilities reduces the sample size by about 26\%.
- The coefficient remains insignificant.
- The coefficient is almost unchanged after winsorization: 0.292 vs. 0.290.


## Overall Conclusion

\small

**Main finding**

- We do not find strong evidence that more negative 10-K tone predicts lower filing-window CAR.
- The coefficient on $\texttt{LM\_NegTone}$ is insignificant in the baseline model and robustness tests.

\vspace{0.2cm}

**What the results suggest**

- The stock market does not appear to respond strongly to the level of negative tone in 10-K filings in this sample.
- Negative tone may reflect routine risk disclosure rather than new information.
- Investors may already anticipate much of the information before the filing date.

\vspace{0.2cm}

**Future improvement**

- Construct the text sample after checking CRSP coverage.
- Test tone changes rather than only tone levels.
- Explore more granular 10-K sections, such as Item 1A Risk Factors and MD&A.
- Use alternative tone measures, including LLM-based measures.
